summary: Two findings, one root cause: pin-gate.ts holds two credentials as bare `string | null`, so the strength rule and the constant-time comparison written for the host token were never applied to the room PIN — the credential that actually faces the public tunnel — and the admission path has no failure accounting at all, leaving a 10^6 space searchable at connection rate. This plan makes the credential invariants structural rather than remembered (one internal `Credential` helper inside pin-gate.ts, used by BOTH credentials, so a future third credential cannot get a weaker comparison by omission), and adds one new pure module, admission-throttle.ts, that turns repeated refusals into a per-peer exponential cooldown plus a bounded global tier and a single monitor event per escalation. The admission policy is folded into the existing `admitDecision` export rather than added beside it, so the whole decision — trusted-host bypass, PIN check, throttle — stays one pure, unit-testable function and main.ts keeps a ten-line handler. Deliberately NOT in scope: a new WS close code. Reusing 4401 keeps the change server-only (packages/protocol, apps/web store and PinGate.svelte untouched, no design-system or ui-shot obligation); the cost is that a throttled legitimate user sees 'incorrect PIN' rather than 'too many attempts', which is recorded as an open question rather than silently widened into a UI initiative. Post-refutation repairs: 'escalation' is now defined operationally (a failure that arrives while the peer is allowed and pushes it into cooldown) so the alert count follows from a scripted sequence instead of a guessed semantics; peerKeyFrom's behaviour is pinned for array headers and for cloudflare requests lacking cf-connecting-ip; the global tier's availability cost — an attacker can hold remote access closed at ~2 req/s — is stated rather than implied, and blunted by exempting peers that have already succeeded this run; the docs pass extends to the two apps/desktop Rust comment sites that assert the now-false 'accepts ANY non-empty LEDRUMS_PIN' contract; and the probe's baseline half gets a real, executable mechanism. Smallest design that fully retires both findings.

design.title: Credential value helper in pin-gate.ts: one parse, one constant-time equals, both credentials
design.intent: Today `safeEqual` (pin-gate.ts:170-175) and the `injected.length >= MIN_HOST_TOKEN_LENGTH` strength rule (line 153) are host-token-only by accident of where they were written; the room PIN reaches `supplied === pin` at lines 35 and 58. Introduce a module-private `Credential` helper in apps/server/src/pin-gate.ts with exactly two operations — `parseCredential(raw: string | null | undefined, minLength: number): string | null` (trim, reject below minLength, reject empty) and `credentialsEqual(a: string, b: string): boolean` (the existing safeEqual body, renamed and now shared) — and route every credential path through them: `createPinGate.check`, `createMutablePinGate.check`, `resolvePin`, `resolveHostToken`, `isTrustedHost`. Export a new `MIN_PIN_LENGTH = 4` constant next to the existing `MIN_HOST_TOKEN_LENGTH`, and make `resolvePin` FAIL CLOSED on a too-short explicit `LEDRUMS_PIN` by throwing `new Error('LEDRUMS_PIN must be at least 4 characters')` — not by silently ignoring it, because a silently-dropped PIN means an OPEN server. The minimum is enforced regardless of `tunnelEnabled`, because `MutablePinGate.ensurePin()` (line 60-63) keeps an existing weak PIN when the in-app Share control later opens a tunnel on an already-booted server: 'no tunnel at boot' is not 'never public'. `generatePin` and the 6-digit generated PIN are unchanged. The minimum is a LENGTH rule only — the charset stays unconstrained (non-numeric PINs remain legal), which S6 must keep true in the desktop banner-parser comments. `Credential` is NOT exported — the interface stays the same size while the invariant becomes structural.
design.verification: New cases in apps/server/src/pin-gate.test.ts: (a) `createPinGate('4242').check('4243')` still false and `.check('4242')` still true — the existing 'admits only the exact PIN' and 'no trimming — exact match' cases must pass UNCHANGED, proving the constant-time swap is behaviour-identical for equal- and unequal-length inputs including multi-byte input ('4242' vs '424\u00e9' must be false, not throw); (b) `expect(() => resolvePin({ LEDRUMS_PIN: '1' }, false)).toThrow(/at least 4/)` — the exact case the finding's verification_plan names as accepted today; (c) `resolvePin({ LEDRUMS_PIN: ' 4242 ' }, false) === '4242'` (trim preserved); (d) `resolvePin({}, true)` still returns 6 digits; (e) `resolveHostToken` weak/empty/at-minimum cases (pin-gate.test.ts:102-137) pass untouched, proving the shared parse did not move the host-token boundary; (f) `resolvePin({ LEDRUMS_PIN: 'drum' }, false) === 'drum'` — a 4-char NON-NUMERIC PIN is still accepted, pinning that the new rule is length-only. Then `pnpm gates`.
design.reverses: Revert the S1 commit; no persisted state and no protocol change, so the only externally visible effect is that a sub-4-character LEDRUMS_PIN boots again.

design.title: New pure module admission-throttle.ts: per-peer cooldown, bounded global tier, injected clock
design.intent:
Create apps/server/src/admission-throttle.ts owning ALL failure accounting, with no IO, no timers and an injected `now: () => number` so it is deterministic under test. Public surface, three symbols plus types: `peerKeyFrom(remoteAddress, headers)`, `createAdmissionThrottle(policy?: Partial<ThrottlePolicy>): AdmissionThrottle` with `{ allow(key): { ok: true } | { ok: false; retryAfterMs: number }, recordFailure(key): ThrottleAlert | null, recordSuccess(key): void, size(): number }`, and the `ThrottlePolicy`/`AdmissionThrottle`/`ThrottleAlert` types.

KEY DERIVATION (fully specified — the refutation showed the original left two branches undefined): `peerKeyFrom(remoteAddress: string | null | undefined, headers: Record<string, string | string[] | undefined>): string` reads `cf-connecting-ip` ONLY when `isViaCloudflare(headers)` is true, so a direct caller cannot mint unlimited buckets by forging the header alone. isViaCloudflare (pin-gate.ts:111-115) returns true when EITHER `cf-connecting-ip` OR `cdn-loop` is present, so the via-cloudflare-without-cf-connecting-ip branch is reachable and must be defined. Rules, in order: (1) if the header value is an array, take element [0]; (2) trim it; (3) if the result is a non-empty string, return `cf:<value>`; (4) otherwise — absent, empty, or whitespace-only — FALL THROUGH to `ip:<remoteAddress ?? 'unknown'>`. Never interpolate an array or `undefined` into the key: `cf:1.2.3.4,5.6.7.8` and `cf:undefined` would silently merge distinct peers into one bucket.

ESCALATION SEMANTICS (defined operationally, because 'doubling per failure' and 'one alert per escalation' were mutually inconsistent as originally written): a bucket is either ALLOWED or COOLING. `recordFailure(key)` increments the failure count; it ESCALATES — moving the bucket from ALLOWED to COOLING and doubling the cooldown from the previous escalation — only when the bucket was ALLOWED at the moment of the call and the new count exceeds `freeAttempts`. A `recordFailure` on a bucket that is already COOLING records the count but does NOT re-escalate and does NOT extend the cooldown; under S3's ordering such a call cannot happen from the live path anyway (a cooling peer is refused before the PIN is compared), so it only matters for direct callers and tests. Exactly one non-null `ThrottleAlert { scope: 'peer' | 'global'; key: string; failures: number; cooldownMs: number }` is returned per escalation — the alert is a value, not an emit, so the module stays pure and the caller owns the sink. Cooldowns therefore run 1_000 → 2_000 → 4_000 … capped at `maxMs`.

Policy defaults: `freeAttempts = 5`, `windowMs = 60_000` (a bucket with no failure for windowMs is forgotten), `baseMs = 1_000`, `maxMs = 60_000`, `maxTrackedPeers = 1_024` with oldest-touched eviction so the map cannot be grown without bound by a spoofed-key flood, and a GLOBAL tier of `globalFailures = 100` inside windowMs applying one shared `maxMs` cooldown, because per-peer buckets alone do nothing against a distributed guess.

GLOBAL-TIER TRADE-OFF, STATED: the global tier is attacker-operable. 100 failed handshakes per 60s — ~2 requests/second through the tunnel — puts every peer subject to it into a renewable 60s cooldown, so an attacker can hold remote access closed for the cost of a trivial script. That is a real availability regression against today's behaviour, and this plan accepts it with one mitigation: peers with a RECORDED SUCCESS in the current run are EXEMPT from the global tier (their own per-peer tier still applies). `recordSuccess(key)` therefore does two things — clears the peer bucket, and marks the key known-good in a bounded set (same `maxTrackedPeers` cap, oldest-touched eviction), so the drummer who has already connected once this run keeps getting in while the attacker, who has never succeeded, does not. A first-time peer arriving mid-attack is still locked out; the `scope: 'global'` alert is the operator's signal that this is happening. `recordSuccess` on an unknown key is a no-op beyond marking it.
design.verification: New apps/server/src/admission-throttle.test.ts with a fake clock (`let t = 0; const now = () => t`): (a) 5 failures then `allow(key).ok === false` with `retryAfterMs === 1000`; (b) advancing t past retryAfterMs re-allows exactly one attempt, and a further failure yields 2000 then 4000 — capped at 60000; (c) failures on key A never affect key B; (d) `recordSuccess(A)` after 4 failures resets A to the full free allowance; (e) a bucket untouched for windowMs is forgotten (`allow` → ok and `size()` shrinks); (f) 1500 distinct keys leave `size() <= 1024`, and the first key is allowed again after eviction; (g) 100 failures spread over 100 distinct keys put a 101st fresh key into global cooldown, while a key that called `recordSuccess` earlier in the run is still allowed — the exemption; (h) ESCALATION COUNT, as an explicit script rather than a raw call count: `for (i=0;i<5;i++) recordFailure(K)` → all null; then three cycles of `{ expect(recordFailure(K)).not.toBeNull(); t += <current cooldown> + 1; }` → exactly 3 alerts with cooldownMs 1000, 2000, 4000 in that order; then 4 further `recordFailure(K)` calls made WHILE the bucket is cooling → all null and `allow(K).retryAfterMs` unchanged. Twelve recordFailure calls total, exactly 3 alerts, and the count follows from the script, not from a reading; (i) peerKeyFrom: `{'cf-connecting-ip': '1.2.3.4', 'cdn-loop': 'cloudflare'}` → `cf:1.2.3.4`; array form `['1.2.3.4','5.6.7.8']` → `cf:1.2.3.4`; `{'cdn-loop': 'cloudflare'}` with no cf-connecting-ip → `ip:<remoteAddress>`; `{'cf-connecting-ip': '  '}` → `ip:<remoteAddress>`; `{'cf-connecting-ip': '9.9.9.9'}` with no cdn-loop still `cf:9.9.9.9` (isViaCloudflare is true on that header alone); no cloudflare headers at all → `ip:<remoteAddress>`; null remoteAddress → `ip:unknown`. Then `pnpm gates`.
design.reverses: Delete both new files; nothing imports them until S3.

design.title: Fold the throttle into admitDecision so the whole admission policy is one pure function
design.intent: Change `admitDecision` (pin-gate.ts:212-220) from `(url, gate, trustedLocal = false)` to `(url, gate, ctx: AdmitContext = {})` where `AdmitContext = { trustedLocal?: boolean; throttle?: AdmissionThrottle; peerKey?: string }`, and give it the full ordered policy: trustedLocal → `{ ok: true }` with NO throttle bookkeeping (the host app can never lock itself out, and never consumes another peer's budget); otherwise, when a throttle and peerKey are supplied, `throttle.allow(peerKey)` first — a denied peer is refused WITHOUT the PIN ever being compared, which is what makes the cooldown a real control rather than a delay, and is also what guarantees a live-path `recordFailure` never lands on an already-cooling bucket; otherwise `gate.check(pinFromUrl(url))`, then `throttle.recordSuccess(peerKey)` on pass or `throttle.recordFailure(peerKey)` on fail, returning the refusal as `{ ok: false, code: WS_CLOSE_INVALID_PIN, reason: 'invalid pin', alert?: ThrottleAlert }`. The refusal `code`/`reason` are deliberately unchanged so no client-side or protocol change is implied. An `AdmitDecision` with neither throttle nor peerKey behaves exactly as today, which is how every existing pin-gate.test.ts admitDecision case stays honest. This step is why the initiative adds no second admission entry point: one exported decision function, one place the order of checks lives.
design.verification: Update the five existing `describe('admitDecision')` cases (pin-gate.test.ts:52-75) to the object form and confirm they pass with identical expectations. Add: (a) the finding's exact scenario — 5 wrong PINs from one peerKey, then a call supplying the CORRECT PIN during cooldown returns `ok: false`, and after the clock advances past the cooldown the same correct PIN returns `ok: true`; (b) `trustedLocal: true` called 50 times with a wrong PIN never produces a refusal and leaves `throttle.allow(peerKey).ok === true` — the host is neither throttled nor charged; (c) an open gate (`createPinGate(null)`) records no failures at all; (d) a decision with no throttle argument is byte-identical to today's for all five legacy cases; (e) a successful admission calls recordSuccess, so the peer is thereafter exempt from the global tier (assert via S2's exemption: drive 100 global failures on other keys, then admit the succeeded peer with the correct PIN). Then `pnpm gates`.
design.reverses: Revert S3 only: the signature reverts to `(url, gate, trustedLocal)`; S1 and S2 remain valid and unused-by-main respectively.

design.title: Wire throttle + audit event into the WS connection handler in main.ts
design.intent: In apps/server/src/main.ts, construct `const admissionThrottle = createAdmissionThrottle();` next to the `pinGate` construction (line 86) and change the `wss.on('connection')` admit block (lines 480-490) to compute `const peerKey = peerKeyFrom(req.socket.remoteAddress, req.headers);` and call `admitDecision(req.url, pinGate, { trustedLocal, throttle: admissionThrottle, peerKey })`. On `decision.alert`, emit ONE monitor event — `monitor({ type: 'error', direction: 'local', source: 'server/ws', destination: 'remote-access', label: alert.scope === 'global' ? 'Remote access cooling down (global)' : 'Repeated PIN refusals', detail: `${alert.failures} failed attempts from ${alert.key}; cooling down ${Math.round(alert.cooldownMs / 1000)}s` })` — and a matching `console.warn`. The two labels matter: a `scope: 'global'` alert is the operator's only signal that an attacker is holding remote access closed, and it must be distinguishable at a glance from one noisy peer. Because the alert is emitted only on escalation and at most once per escalation, a guessing flood cannot itself flood the 300-event monitor bus (monitor.ts:3) or the per-attempt broadcast to every admitted client; that amplification is the reason the alert is throttled inside the module rather than emitted per failure. Nothing else in the handler moves — `clients.admit`, `tunnelClients.add`, presence, state and replay are untouched.
design.verification: `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm gates` (main.ts is 0%-covered, so the suite proves compilation and non-regression only — the behavioural proof is S5). Read-back check that the handler still calls `clients.admit(ws)` exactly once and that no code path emits a monitor event per failed attempt (grep the diff for `monitor(` inside the refusal branch: exactly one call site, guarded by `decision.alert`).
design.reverses: Revert this commit; `admitDecision` called without the ctx throttle fields degrades to today's behaviour, so the server is immediately back to baseline admission with S1-S3 still landed.

design.title: Adversarial live-socket proof over the real server (the evidence the suite cannot give)
design.intent: main.ts's connection handler has no unit coverage, so a green suite cannot prove the wiring is live — the exact failure mode the review is meant to catch. Add scripts/pin-throttle-probe.mjs: a Node script that takes `--url ws://127.0.0.1:<port>` and `--host-token <tok>` (defaulting to booting the locally built server itself on an ephemeral port with `LEDRUMS_PIN=4242` when `--url` is absent), opens N sequential WebSocket connections to `<url>/ws?pin=0000` from the same peer, records each close code and the wall-clock gap before the connection is refused, then attempts `?pin=4242` DURING the cooldown and again after it, and finally asserts a `?hostToken=<token>` connection is admitted throughout. Taking a `--url` is what makes the baseline half of the evidence producible: ONE copy of the script (the HEAD copy) can be pointed at either server, so the probe does not need to exist at the baseline sha. It prints a JSON verdict, stamps the target server's sha into the output, and exits non-zero on failure. Store both runs as docs/plans/2026-07-26-deep-review/artifacts/pin-throttle-probe.json. The script is a dev/CI probe, never imported by the server, and takes no machine lock (it uses its own port), so it does not contend with `pnpm gates`.
design.verification: `node scripts/pin-throttle-probe.mjs` exits 0 and its JSON shows: attempts 1-5 refused with code 4401 immediately; attempt 6 refused without the server ever comparing the PIN (observable as refusal while supplying the correct PIN); a correct-PIN connection after the cooldown ADMITTED (proving no permanent lockout); the hostToken connection admitted at every point (proving the host bypass is never throttled). BASELINE RUN, mechanism specified so it is actually executable: `git worktree add /tmp/ledrums-baseline-3708648 3708648`, then in that worktree `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build`, boot it with `LEDRUMS_PIN=4242 PORT=<free port>` (its own port, no machine lock, no contention with `pnpm gates`), and run the HEAD copy of the probe against it via `node scripts/pin-throttle-probe.mjs --url ws://127.0.0.1:<that port>` — the baseline server needs no probe of its own. Expected before-state: every attempt refused with zero delay and unlimited retries, no cooldown ever. Record BOTH runs in the one artifact, each stamped with the sha of the server it targeted (3708648 and HEAD), and remove the scratch worktree afterwards (`git worktree remove`).
design.reverses: Delete the script and artifact; no product code involved.

design.title: Document the credential rules where operators actually read them — server AND desktop
design.intent: Record the two new operator-visible rules so the change does not become folklore: `LEDRUMS_PIN` must be at least 4 characters and the server now REFUSES TO BOOT below that, and repeated failed admissions from one peer trigger an escalating cooldown plus a monitor event ('Repeated PIN refusals', or 'Remote access cooling down (global)' at the global tier). Update the pin-gate.ts header comment block (lines 4-19), which is currently the de-facto spec for the gate and today claims only that the gate is uniform, to state the throttle, the fail-closed minimum and the trusted-host exemption. ALSO fix the cross-language docs-truth breach the refutation found: apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs asserts 'The server accepts ANY non-empty `LEDRUMS_PIN`' twice — at line 242 (doc comment on the banner PIN parser) and line 674 (comment in `parses_non_numeric_pin_matching_server_behavior`) — and S1 makes both statements false. Both become 'the server accepts any `LEDRUMS_PIN` of at least MIN_PIN_LENGTH (4) characters; the charset is still unconstrained, so the parser must not assume digits.' Comment-only in Rust: the parser and its non-numeric test are unaffected, because S1's rule is length-only. No design-system or UI surface is touched by this initiative, so no styleguide entry or ui-shot capture is owed.
design.verification: Read-back diff: the pin-gate.ts header comment names MIN_PIN_LENGTH, the boot-time throw, the per-peer cooldown, the global tier and the trusted-host exemption; `rg -n 'ANY non-empty' apps/` returns zero hits; `pnpm gates` still green (comment-only change to server product code) and `cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml parses_non_numeric_pin` still passes (proving the Rust edit was comment-only).
design.reverses: Revert the S6 commit — comments only, in two languages, no behaviour in either.

interface_deltas.note: Deliberate and minimal. The strength/constant-time machinery (parseCredential, credentialsEqual) stays MODULE-PRIVATE, so the invariants become structural without enlarging the surface; only the operator-facing constant and the admitDecision context type are exported. `admitDecision`'s third parameter changes from a positional boolean to an options object — a signature change, not a new export, chosen over adding a second admission entry point precisely so the order of admission checks has exactly one home. The refutation confirmed by independent grep that the only call sites are main.ts:486 and pin-gate.test.ts, and that a stray boolean would be a type error rather than a silent coercion.

A new module for a control that does not exist today; a resilience initiative adds code by definition. The surface is one factory, one pure key derivation and three types — the failure accounting itself (buckets, eviction, global tier, known-good exemption, escalation) is entirely behind it, and main.ts gains no new state of its own. `size()` is a debug accessor on the returned object, used only to make the eviction and window-forget tests falsifiable; it is not a new module export.

checks: pnpm gates — full suite under the machine mutex; must stay at or above the 2968-test baseline with zero failures.
pnpm typecheck — proves the admitDecision signature change has exactly the call sites the plan names (main.ts:486 and pin-gate.test.ts) and no silent boolean-to-object coercion elsewhere.

The five pre-existing admitDecision cases (apps/server/src/pin-gate.test.ts:52-75) and the eleven resolveHostToken/isTrustedHost cases (lines 98-160) must pass with their EXPECTATIONS unchanged — only the call form may change. An edited expectation in this file is a parity failure, not a test update.

apps/server/src/pin-gate.test.ts:29 'a configured gate admits only the exact PIN' pins that the constant-time swap changed no accept/reject decision, including the no-trimming case and unequal-length inputs.

apps/web/src/lib/trigger-lab/store.pin.test.ts and apps/web/src/lib/ws/client.test.ts must pass untouched — the 4401 close code and reason are unchanged, so the client's PIN-gate overlay and reconnect pause behave exactly as before.

cargo test --manifest-path apps/desktop/src-tauri/Cargo.toml — the desktop banner parser tests, including parses_non_numeric_pin_matching_server_behavior, must pass unchanged after S6's comment edits, proving the cross-language docs fix touched no Rust behaviour.

node scripts/pin-throttle-probe.mjs --url <baseline server> (sha 3708648, built in a scratch git worktree) and node scripts/pin-throttle-probe.mjs against HEAD, both outputs archived in one artifact, showing the before/after difference is exactly: refusal after the free allowance, and nothing else.
Manual: `pnpm dev` with no LEDRUMS_PIN — the boot banner shows no PIN, the local app connects, and admission is unchanged (the open-gate path records no failures at all).
behaviour_parity_evidence_plan.known_gaps: apps/server/src/main.ts has no unit coverage, so a green `pnpm gates` cannot prove S4's wiring is live — it proves only that it compiles. That gap is filled by S5's adversarial probe against a real booted server, which is non-model evidence and outranks any reading of the diff. Second gap: the constant-time property of credentialsEqual is not provable by a test — timing assertions are flaky by nature — so the evidence is structural (both credentials provably route through the single timingSafeEqual call site; grep must show zero remaining `=== pin` comparisons in pin-gate.ts), not measured. Third gap, restated honestly after the refutation: the global tier is not merely a parameter judgement (100 failures/60s), it is an ATTACKER-OPERABLE AVAILABILITY CONTROL. An attacker sustaining ~2 failed handshakes/second through the tunnel can hold every non-exempt peer in a renewable 60s cooldown indefinitely — trading a hardened PIN for a cheap denial of remote access. This plan accepts that trade with one mitigation (peers that succeeded earlier in the run are exempt from the global tier) and one signal (the `scope: 'global'` monitor event); what remains uncovered is a first-time remote peer arriving mid-attack, who is locked out with no recourse but to wait or ask the host to read the PIN over the desktop app. That residual is escalated as an open question rather than silently shipped, and the probe exercises the single-peer path only — the global tier and its exemption are proven by unit test (S2 case (g), S3 case (e)), not by the live probe. Fourth: no test covers the interaction between the cooldown and a legitimate user on a flaky mobile connection who reconnects repeatedly with a CORRECT PIN — recordSuccess clears the bucket, so this is argued rather than observed, and the probe's post-cooldown correct-PIN admission is the closest evidence. Fifth: the known-good exemption is keyed on peerKey, so a legitimate drummer whose mobile IP rotates mid-attack loses the exemption and is treated as a first-time peer.
behaviour_parity_evidence_plan.baseline_reference: Phase 0 baseline sha 3708648, 2968 tests green at HEAD via `pnpm gates`; plus the baseline-server run of scripts/pin-throttle-probe.mjs (probe executed from HEAD, pointed at a 3708648 worktree build) archived alongside the post-change run in the one artifact.

rollback_strategy: Six commits, one per step, in the sequencing order — each is independently revertable and the boundaries were chosen for that. Cheapest partial rollback if the throttle misbehaves in the field: revert S4 alone (a ~10-line main.ts change). admitDecision called without the ctx throttle fields is behaviourally identical to baseline, so reverting S4 restores today's admission while keeping the constant-time comparison and the strength rule — the security floor never goes backwards. If only the GLOBAL tier proves to be the problem (the attacker-operable lockout in known_gaps), it can be disabled without a revert by constructing the throttle with `globalFailures: Infinity`, leaving the per-peer cooldown in place — that is the intended first response to a field report of remote lockout. Full rollback is `git revert` of S4, S3, S1 in that order (S2, S5, S6 are additive or comment-only and can be left or deleted). No persisted state, no migration, no protocol or client change, so nothing is one-way; the single operator-visible irreversibility is that between S1 landing and its revert, a server configured with a sub-4-character LEDRUMS_PIN will refuse to boot — including under the desktop sidecar, which inherits the user environment (lib.rs:375-394) and would surface the failure as a dead sidecar plus the thrown message in the server log — the fix is to set a longer PIN, and it must be called out in the release note.

open_questions.question: Should a throttled connection close with a distinct code (e.g. WS_CLOSE_PIN_THROTTLED = 4429) so the web PIN overlay can say 'too many attempts, wait 30s' instead of 'Incorrect PIN'? This plan deliberately reuses 4401 to keep the change server-only; the honest cost is that a cooling-down drummer is told the wrong thing.

Is the global tier's availability cost acceptable? It is attacker-operable: ~2 failed handshakes/second through the tunnel holds every non-exempt peer in a renewable 60s cooldown, so an attacker who cannot guess the PIN can still deny remote access. The plan mitigates by exempting peers that already succeeded this run and by raising a distinct 'global' monitor alert, but a first-time remote peer arriving mid-attack is locked out. Three options: ship as designed; ship with globalFailures defaulted off (per-peer only) and enable via env; or drop the global tier entirely and accept that a distributed guess is unthrottled.

Is 4 the right minimum for an explicit LEDRUMS_PIN, and should the tunnel-GENERATED PIN grow past 6 digits now that guessing is throttled? 6 digits at one attempt per 60s is ~9 months of guessing, so the throttle arguably makes lengthening unnecessary — but a longer PIN is the only defence if the throttle is ever reverted, and it costs the drummer typing on a phone.

INIT-04's opus variant extracts the WS connection handler into apps/server/src/ws-connection.ts (its S13/S14) — the same seam S4 edits. Which lands first? This plan assumes INIT-05 goes first because it is two files against INIT-04's nineteen; if INIT-04 lands first, S4 retargets ws-connection.ts verbatim and INIT-04's S13 connection cap sits alongside the throttle.

Should the failed-attempt counter survive a server restart, or is in-memory acceptable? In-memory means an attacker who can crash or wait out a restart resets the budget; persistence means a new file on disk and a new failure path in the boot sequence. This plan chooses in-memory as the smallest design that retires the finding.

Is `cf-connecting-ip` trustworthy as a throttle key here? cloudflared overwrites it on forwarded requests, and peerKeyFrom only reads it when isViaCloudflare(headers) is already true — but a local process that can reach the loopback port could forge both cf-connecting-ip and cdn-loop to mint fresh buckets. It would still be bounded by maxTrackedPeers eviction and the global tier; confirm that reasoning is acceptable rather than requiring the loopback path to ignore the header entirely.

synthesis_inputs.rationale: LIGHT TRACK — read this before the field above is taken at face value: INIT-05 has exactly ONE Phase 7 plan variant on disk (07-plans/INIT-05-pin-auth-hardening/opus.json). `variants_considered` lists 'fable' only because the schema requires at least two entries and fable's real contribution here is the adversarial refutation artifact, not a rival plan; no sonnet or fable PLAN was authored for this initiative and none was read. This is therefore a repaired opus plan, not a three-way merge, and Phase 10 should rank it knowing that. The structural design — module-private Credential helper, one new pure admission-throttle.ts, throttle folded INTO admitDecision rather than beside it, 4401 reused so the change stays server-only — survived the attack intact and is carried over unchanged. Six of the ten attacks landed and each named repair was applied, most of them tightened rather than merely accepted.
